name: English IV - Advanced Composition / Media Writing
nameZh: 英语四高级写作与媒体
description: A senior English course focusing on advanced composition and professional media writing across genres including feature journalism, opinion writing, script writing, and digital publishing.

modules.objectives: Review and apply advanced composition principles including thesis development, argumentation, evidence integration, and revision at a senior level. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Writing Guide 1.1 — rhetorical situation, audience, purpose, context, and responsible response for advanced composition review.

modules.assignment: Revise this fictional editorial draft: “North Harbor Library should stay open later. Students need it. The library is useful and many people study there. A survey says 62% of 240 respondents lack a quiet weekday study place after 6 p.m. The plan could use rotating staff. Some people say it costs too much, but learning matters. Therefore the library should stay open.” Produce a 450–550 word revision and an editor memo. Submit: one labeled document. Include: a precise thesis, logical paragraph plan, responsible use of the survey, a response to the cost concern, and annotations explaining three revisions. Evaluation: argument/logic 30%; audience and genre 30%; evidence 25%; clarity/mechanics 15%.

modules.assignment: Use this fictional North Harbor bus-pass packet: 480 students commute; 38% of 320 survey respondents missed at least one first period last month because of transportation; a six-week pilot would provide 120 passes at $24 each; the transit agency offers a 10% bulk discount; attendance staff would track only aggregate results; administrators worry about cost and fair eligibility. Write three versions for a student blog, an administrator memo, and a newspaper letter; do not send or publish them. Submit: one labeled document. Include: the same verified facts in all versions, audience-specific tone/structure, a recommendation, one limitation, and annotations explaining five adaptations. Evaluation: factual consistency 25%; audience adaptation 35%; reasoning 25%; clarity 15%.

modules.assignment: Write a 650–750 word profile of fictional robotics mentor Maya Chen. Fact card: Chen is 29, studied mechanical engineering, volunteers Saturdays at North Harbor Youth Lab, built a low-cost sensor kit from recycled parts, and coached a team that completed 11 prototypes in 2025. Quotations: Chen—“A failed prototype is a map of what to test next.” Student Luis Ortega—“She asks us to explain the evidence before she offers a fix.” Lab director Priya Raman—“Maya made the workshop feel rigorous and welcoming at the same time.” Do not research or identify a real person. Submit: one labeled document. Include: a focused angle, scene-setting opening, all three attributed quotations, factual background, and an editor note distinguishing fact from description. Evaluation: angle/structure 30%; reporting accuracy 30%; quotation integration 25%; style 15%.

modules.assignment: Write a 550–650 word opinion column on this fictional proposal: replace one of North Harbor's four parking lots with a public garden. Supporting evidence: the lot averaged 22% occupancy across 20 school days; the garden plan adds 32 trees, 18 accessible beds, and two outdoor-class tables; a grant would cover $38,000 of the $52,000 start-up cost. Opposing evidence: peak-event parking would fall by 86 spaces; annual maintenance is estimated at $7,500; accessibility advocates request a paved drop-off zone. Submit: one labeled document. Include: a clear position, at least three packet facts, fair counterargument, practical response, and call to action; do not conduct outside advocacy. Evaluation: claim/reasoning 30%; evidence 30%; counterargument 25%; style 15%.

modules.assignment: Write a 650–750 word narrative report about this fictional community-center outage. Timeline: 7:42 p.m. lights flickered; 7:45 power failed; 7:49 staff opened two emergency-light cabinets; 7:58 all 63 visitors reached the courtyard; 8:21 utility crews identified a failed transformer; 9:36 power returned. Quotes: visitor Ana Ruiz—“The room went quiet before the phone lights appeared.” Coordinator Devon Hale—“We counted every group twice before giving the all-clear.” Utility spokesperson Mina Cho—“The failure was confined to one transformer.” Verified facts: no injuries, indoor temperature 74°F, two exits remained open. Submit: one labeled document. Include: a scene, accurate chronology, all quotes with attribution, no invented observations, evidence-based reasoning that connects details to the story angle, and a 100-word verification note. Evaluation: factual accuracy 35%; narrative craft 30%; attribution 20%; verification note 15%.

modules.assignment: Investigate this fictional cafeteria-waste case. Waste log: edible discarded food averaged 46 kg/day in Week 1 and 39 kg/day in Week 2 after smaller default portions; measurements cover five days each. Budget memo: food purchases were $9,800 in Week 1 and $9,250 in Week 2, but enrollment fell 3%. Staff interview: manager Lena Park said, “Students may request a second portion at no charge,” and warned that two Week 2 deliveries were smaller than planned. Write a 600-word findings report; do not contact anyone. Submit: one labeled document. Include: a quantified trend, source-by-source reliability check, two alternative explanations, a qualified conclusion, and two follow-up records that would be needed. Evaluation: document use 35%; causal caution 25%; organization 25%; clarity 15%.

modules.assignment: Create draft-only social posts for the fictional nonprofit Green Block. Mission: turn vacant neighborhood lots into accessible community gardens and donate produce locally. Verified facts: Green Block maintains 8 gardens, worked with 120 volunteers last year, and donated 2,400 pounds of produce. Campaign goal: recruit 40 volunteers for an October 12 cleanup. Available fictional images show (1) seedlings in labeled trays, (2) gloves beside hand tools, (3) an accessible raised bed, (4) produce on a scale, and (5) a volunteer group with no names shown. Draft five image captions, a five-post thread, and one professional-network post; do not create an account or publish. Submit: one labeled document. Include: accurate packet evidence, evidence-based reasoning for each call to action, platform-specific calls to action, alt text for each image, one consistent voice guide, and annotations explaining three adaptations. modules.assignment: Write three 300–400 word sample posts for a fictional study-skills site using this packet. In an eight-week school pilot, 80 volunteers were split evenly: the spaced-practice group completed four 20-minute sessions each week and averaged 78% on a delayed quiz; the one-session group studied for the same total weekly time and averaged 69%. The pilot was not randomized and prior achievement was not reported. Student Noor Patel said, “Short sessions were easier to schedule, but I still needed reminders.” Create (1) a how-to for planning spaced sessions, (2) an evidence-based opinion on whether the school should test the approach more widely, and (3) a third-person narrative about fictional student Eli trying the schedule. Avoid personal disclosure. Submit: one labeled document. Include: accurate packet evidence, headings and links described without publishing, a limitation in the opinion post, and annotations explaining genre choices. For each post, add a private SEO planning note that states the reader’s search intent, one accurate primary key phrase, an honest search-title draft, and a 140–160 character meta-description draft; do not publish or make ranking claims. Evaluation: evidence accuracy 30%; genre control 30%; reasoning 25%; clarity 15%.

modules.assignment: Use this fictional school-board packet. Draft a 90-second news script and a three-minute podcast script. Do not record or contact real people. Submit: one labeled document. Include: accurate lead, attributed quotes, timing labels, sound cues only where justified, and a note explaining differences between the formats. Evaluation: accuracy 35%; writing for the ear 30%; format adaptation 25%; clarity 10%.

quizQuestions.question: Advanced composition differs from introductory writing primarily in its emphasis on:
options: Basic grammar rules and paragraph structure
Nuanced thesis development, complex argumentation, and sophisticated style
Learning to write the five-paragraph essay
Avoiding all use of research sources
quizQuestions.answer: Nuanced thesis development, complex argumentation, and sophisticated style
quizQuestions.explanation: Advanced composition builds on foundational skills, demanding more sophisticated thesis development, complex argumentation, and intentional stylistic choices.

quizQuestions.question: Evaluating your own previous writing for thesis clarity requires asking:
options: Is this essay long enough?
Does my thesis make a specific, debatable claim that my body paragraphs actually prove?
Did I use enough quotations?
Is every sentence grammatically correct?
quizQuestions.answer: Does my thesis make a specific, debatable claim that my body paragraphs actually prove?
quizQuestions.explanation: Thesis evaluation checks whether the thesis is specific, debatable, and whether the essay's body paragraphs actually develop and prove that exact claim.

quizQuestions.question: Which revision most strengthens a vague thesis?
options: Name the specific claim, stakes, and conditions the essay will defend
Add two broad adjectives without changing the claim
Replace the thesis with a quotation
Move the same vague sentence to the conclusion
quizQuestions.answer: Name the specific claim, stakes, and conditions the essay will defend
quizQuestions.explanation: A strong revision clarifies the position, why it matters, and any needed limits so the body can prove it. Added adjectives, a borrowed quotation, or relocation leave the thesis's reasoning vague.

quizQuestions.question: Which revision strategy most improves coherence between paragraphs?
options: Add a transition that names the logical relationship
Repeat the thesis word for word
Remove every topic sentence
Change all verbs to passive voice
quizQuestions.answer: Add a transition that names the logical relationship
quizQuestions.explanation: A precise transition shows whether ideas extend, contrast, or cause one another.

quizQuestions.question: Audience analysis requires writers to consider:
options: Only the reader's age and grade level
The reader's background knowledge, values, expectations, and needs
Only whether the reader agrees with the writer's position
Only the format in which they will read the text
quizQuestions.answer: The reader's background knowledge, values, expectations, and needs
quizQuestions.explanation: Effective audience analysis considers background knowledge, values, interests, expectations, and what the audience needs from the text.

quizQuestions.question: A formal memo differs from a blog post primarily in:
options: The topic covered
Register, format, length, and level of formality appropriate to its professional context
Whether it includes images
Whether it requires citations
quizQuestions.answer: Register, format, length, and level of formality appropriate to its professional context
quizQuestions.explanation: A memo is a professional document with formal register and specific formatting conventions, while a blog is conversational and less structurally constrained.

quizQuestions.question: A letter to the editor in a local newspaper should be written for an audience that is:
options: Expert academics familiar with advanced scholarly discourse
The general public of the community, with accessible language and concrete local relevance
Only the newspaper's editorial staff
Young children learning to read
quizQuestions.answer: The general public of the community, with accessible language and concrete local relevance
quizQuestions.explanation: Letters to the editor address the general community readership—accessible language, concrete examples, and clear relevance to local concerns are essential.

quizQuestions.question: A transportation proposal is being adapted from an administrator memo to a student blog. Which change best fits the new audience while preserving accuracy?
options: Explain the practical student impact in accessible language while keeping the same verified numbers
Remove all costs because students may dislike them
Change the survey percentage to make the plan more persuasive
Use unexplained policy acronyms to sound authoritative
quizQuestions.answer: Explain the practical student impact in accessible language while keeping the same verified numbers
quizQuestions.explanation: Audience adaptation changes framing, tone, examples, and format while preserving verified facts. Hiding costs, altering data, or adding unexplained jargon weakens trust and does not responsibly address student readers.

quizQuestions.question: Feature writing differs from hard news writing in that feature writing:
options: Reports breaking news as quickly as possible
Uses narrative techniques, depth, and human interest to explore topics in detail
Requires no sources or quotations
Always presents statistical data
quizQuestions.answer: Uses narrative techniques, depth, and human interest to explore topics in detail
quizQuestions.explanation: Feature writing goes beyond reporting immediate events to provide depth, narrative, and human interest through storytelling techniques.

quizQuestions.question: A scene-setting opening in a feature article serves to:
options: Immediately present the article's main statistics
Draw readers in by placing them vividly in a specific moment or setting
List the credentials of the journalist
Summarize all the article's main points
quizQuestions.answer: Draw readers in by placing them vividly in a specific moment or setting
quizQuestions.explanation: Scene-setting opens a feature by immersing the reader in a specific, vivid moment, creating immediate engagement and emotional investment.

quizQuestions.question: A profile feature article focuses on:
options: A product or service review
In-depth exploration of a person through reporting, anecdotes, and quotations
Only positive achievements of the subject
Statistical data about a demographic group
quizQuestions.answer: In-depth exploration of a person through reporting, anecdotes, and quotations
quizQuestions.explanation: A profile feature provides an in-depth, textured portrait of a person through observation, research, anecdotes, and direct quotation.

quizQuestions.question: Which source practice is required when writing a profile from an interview transcript?
options: Attribute quotations to the named speaker
Remove the speaker’s context
Combine two speakers into one without disclosure
Present paraphrases as direct quotations
quizQuestions.answer: Attribute quotations to the named speaker
quizQuestions.explanation: Attribution lets readers distinguish the subject’s words from the writer’s narration.

quizQuestions.question: A strong opinion column is distinguished from a weak one by:
options: Being longer than 1000 words
Having a clear, specific position supported by evidence and addressing counterarguments
Expressing strong emotions throughout
Being written in the third person only
quizQuestions.answer: Having a clear, specific position supported by evidence and addressing counterarguments
quizQuestions.explanation: A strong opinion column takes a specific, defensible position, supports it with evidence and reasoning, and engages thoughtfully with opposing views.

quizQuestions.question: An editorial represents the views of:
options: A single named journalist
The publication's editorial board—the collective voice of the news organization
Anonymous community members
The publication's advertisers
quizQuestions.answer: The publication's editorial board—the collective voice of the news organization
quizQuestions.explanation: An editorial expresses the institutional opinion of the publication's editorial board, unlike opinion columns (bylined) or news reports (objective).

quizQuestions.question: A call to action in an opinion piece:
options: Summarizes the article's main points
Urges the reader to take a specific action in response to the argument
Introduces a new counterargument in the conclusion
Lists all sources used
quizQuestions.answer: Urges the reader to take a specific action in response to the argument
quizQuestions.explanation: A call to action tells readers specifically what they should do—vote, donate, speak out, or change behavior—in response to the argument presented.

quizQuestions.question: Acknowledging the opposing view in an opinion column strengthens the piece by:
options: Undermining the writer's own position
Demonstrating fairness and allowing the writer to refute the counterargument with evidence
Making the column longer to meet word count
Replacing the need for evidence
quizQuestions.answer: Demonstrating fairness and allowing the writer to refute the counterargument with evidence
quizQuestions.explanation: Engaging with the opposing view shows intellectual honesty, strengthens the writer's credibility (ethos), and allows them to rebut the counterargument.

quizQuestions.question: Narrative journalism differs from traditional news reporting primarily in its:
options: Avoidance of factual accuracy
Use of literary storytelling techniques (scene, character, tension, voice) applied to real events
Focus only on fictional events
Lack of direct quotations from sources
quizQuestions.answer: Use of literary storytelling techniques (scene, character, tension, voice) applied to real events
quizQuestions.explanation: Narrative journalism applies novelistic techniques—scene-building, character development, dramatic tension—to factually accurate reporting of real events.

quizQuestions.question: Scene-building in narrative journalism requires:
options: Inventing details to make the story more interesting
Specific, observed sensory details that place the reader in the exact moment being reported
Summarizing the event without any sensory description
Using only official statistics
quizQuestions.answer: Specific, observed sensory details that place the reader in the exact moment being reported
quizQuestions.explanation: Scenes in narrative journalism must be built from observed or reported specific details—journalists cannot invent scenes but must gather them through reporting.

quizQuestions.question: Which feature most clearly distinguishes narrative journalism from a standard breaking-news brief?
options: Scene-based structure supported by verified reporting
The absence of factual verification
Invented quotations presented as real
No attention to chronology
quizQuestions.answer: Scene-based structure supported by verified reporting
quizQuestions.explanation: Narrative journalism uses storytelling techniques while retaining journalistic verification. The other choices do not satisfy the module definition or the evidence in the prompt.

quizQuestions.question: Which detail best builds a scene without overstating what the reporter knows?
options: The room was obviously filled with despair.
At 8:05 p.m., the lights went out and three people raised phone flashlights.
Everyone felt exactly the same emotion.
The event was the worst moment in history.
quizQuestions.answer: At 8:05 p.m., the lights went out and three people raised phone flashlights.
quizQuestions.explanation: Observable, time-specific detail creates a scene without claiming access to every person’s thoughts.

quizQuestions.question: Investigative journalism primarily seeks to:
options: Report breaking events as they happen
Uncover and expose wrongdoing, systemic problems, or hidden information in the public interest
Write profiles of interesting people
Provide entertainment through human interest stories
quizQuestions.answer: Uncover and expose wrongdoing, systemic problems, or hidden information in the public interest
quizQuestions.explanation: Investigative journalism uses in-depth research, document analysis, and source interviews to uncover issues of public importance that are not readily visible.

quizQuestions.question: FOIA (Freedom of Information Act) requests are tools used in investigative journalism to:
options: Get free access to entertainment media
Request access to government records and documents that are legally available to the public
Protect journalists from legal action
Verify the identity of anonymous sources
quizQuestions.answer: Request access to government records and documents that are legally available to the public
quizQuestions.explanation: FOIA allows journalists and citizens to formally request access to federal government records, which must be released unless protected by specific exemptions.

quizQuestions.question: The cafeteria packet shows waste fell from 46 to 39 kg/day, but enrollment also fell 3% and two deliveries were smaller. Which conclusion is most responsible?
options: Smaller default portions caused the entire decline in waste.
The observed decline is real in the logs, but enrollment and delivery changes are alternative explanations that must be checked.
The staff interview proves the waste logs are wrong.
The two weeks establish a permanent trend for every school.
quizQuestions.answer: The observed decline is real in the logs, but enrollment and delivery changes are alternative explanations that must be checked.
quizQuestions.explanation: Investigative writing should report the documented trend while testing rival explanations. The packet does not isolate portion size as the cause, and two weeks at one fictional site cannot establish a universal result.

quizQuestions.question: A waste log declines during the same week that enrollment also falls. What is the most responsible conclusion?
options: The decline is associated with the intervention, but enrollment and delivery changes are alternative explanations
The intervention alone caused every kilogram of reduction
The log proves wrongdoing by cafeteria staff
No conclusion is possible because two variables changed
quizQuestions.answer: The decline is associated with the intervention, but enrollment and delivery changes are alternative explanations
quizQuestions.explanation: The records show a change but do not isolate its cause. A careful report states the association, tests plausible alternatives such as enrollment and delivery volume, and identifies additional evidence needed before making a causal claim.

quizQuestions.question: Before publication, right of reply means a reporter should:
options: Offer a criticized person or organization a fair chance to respond
Promise favorable coverage
Reveal confidential sources
Delete all critical evidence
quizQuestions.answer: Offer a criticized person or organization a fair chance to respond
quizQuestions.explanation: A fair opportunity to respond improves accuracy without giving a subject control of the story.

quizQuestions.question: Professional social media writing differs from personal posting primarily in its:
options: Use of more emoji and casual language
Intentionality about audience, message, voice, and brand consistency
Focus on personal opinions and reactions
Avoidance of all factual content
quizQuestions.answer: Intentionality about audience, message, voice, and brand consistency
quizQuestions.explanation: Professional social media writing is strategic—deliberately crafting message, tone, and format to serve a clear purpose for a specific audience.

quizQuestions.question: Instagram captions for a professional account should:
options: Be as long as possible to maximize information
Be tailored to the platform's visual-first culture: engaging, concise, and aligned with the image
Avoid any use of hashtags
Use formal academic vocabulary
quizQuestions.answer: Be tailored to the platform's visual-first culture: engaging, concise, and aligned with the image
quizQuestions.explanation: Instagram captions support the visual content—they should be engaging and appropriately brief, using relevant hashtags and language suited to the platform's conversational culture.

quizQuestions.question: A professional account should adapt one message across platforms by changing:
options: The verified facts
Length, format, and call to action for each audience
The organization’s identity each time
Whether accuracy matters
quizQuestions.answer: Length, format, and call to action for each audience
quizQuestions.explanation: Platform conventions change presentation, while facts and organizational identity remain consistent.

quizQuestions.question: What creates consistency across an organization’s social posts?
options: A stable voice, visual pattern, and purpose
Using the same sentence in every post
Changing verified facts by platform
Avoiding any audience goal
quizQuestions.answer: A stable voice, visual pattern, and purpose
quizQuestions.explanation: Consistency comes from recognizable choices that still adapt to each platform.

quizQuestions.question: A compelling blog headline should:
options: Be as long as possible to explain the full content
Be specific, intriguing, and promise clear value to the reader
Use only generic words like 'things' or 'stuff'
Always begin with a number
quizQuestions.answer: Be specific, intriguing, and promise clear value to the reader
quizQuestions.explanation: An effective blog headline creates curiosity or promises specific value, using concrete, specific language to draw readers in and indicate what they'll gain.

quizQuestions.question: Subheadings in a blog post serve to:
options: Replace the need for transitional sentences
Break content into scannable sections, helping online readers navigate and find what they need
Make the post look longer
Indicate the writer's level of expertise
quizQuestions.answer: Break content into scannable sections, helping online readers navigate and find what they need
quizQuestions.explanation: Subheadings support online reading behavior—most web readers scan before reading in full, and clear subheadings allow navigation to relevant sections.

quizQuestions.question: A how-to blog post differs from an informative post in that it:
options: Provides general background information without actionable steps
Provides step-by-step guidance enabling the reader to accomplish a specific task
Avoids using numbered lists
Focuses on the writer's personal opinion
quizQuestions.answer: Provides step-by-step guidance enabling the reader to accomplish a specific task
quizQuestions.explanation: A how-to post is instructional—it guides the reader through a specific process step by step, enabling them to replicate it themselves.

quizQuestions.question: Which headline gives the clearest specific value to a reader?
options: Some Thoughts About Studying
Five Ways to Check a Source Before You Share It
Things You Should Know
My Post
quizQuestions.answer: Five Ways to Check a Source Before You Share It
quizQuestions.explanation: It names the task, scope, and benefit in concrete language. The other choices do not satisfy the module definition or the evidence in the prompt.

quizQuestions.question: Writing for the ear (broadcast/podcast) differs from writing for the eye primarily in that:
options: Broadcast writing uses longer, more complex sentences
Broadcast writing uses short, direct sentences and conversational language designed to be heard, not read
Broadcast writing requires more citations than print writing
Print writing is always more formal than broadcast writing
quizQuestions.answer: Broadcast writing uses short, direct sentences and conversational language designed to be heard, not read
quizQuestions.explanation: Broadcast writing is designed for listeners who cannot reread—sentences must be short, clear, and conversational, avoiding complex constructions that work better on paper.

quizQuestions.question: The inverted pyramid structure in broadcast news means:
options: Starting with background information and building to the main point
Leading with the most important information and following with supporting details
Presenting events strictly in chronological order
Using a narrative story structure with a climax
quizQuestions.answer: Leading with the most important information and following with supporting details
quizQuestions.explanation: The inverted pyramid leads with the most newsworthy information (who, what, when, where) and then provides supporting context and details in decreasing order of importance.

quizQuestions.question: A podcast script differs from a broadcast news script in that it:
options: Must be shorter and contain fewer words
Can use a more conversational voice, narrative pacing, and sound design cues appropriate to a longer-form audio format
Cannot include any research or factual content
Must always be read verbatim from the script
quizQuestions.answer: Can use a more conversational voice, narrative pacing, and sound design cues appropriate to a longer-form audio format
quizQuestions.explanation: Podcast scripts allow more conversational, long-form style with sound design cues and narrative pacing suited to an on-demand, intimate audio format.

quizQuestions.question: Why do scriptwriters label sound cues?
options: To guide timing, transitions, and production choices
To replace factual reporting
To hide the speaker identity
To make every segment longer
quizQuestions.answer: To guide timing, transitions, and production choices
quizQuestions.explanation: Sound cues coordinate what listeners hear with the script’s structure. The other choices do not satisfy the module definition or the evidence in the prompt.

quizQuestions.question: A grant proposal's problem statement should:
options: Describe only the proposed solution
Clearly and specifically identify the problem to be addressed and its significance
Be written in the most technical language possible
List the budget first
quizQuestions.answer: Clearly and specifically identify the problem to be addressed and its significance
quizQuestions.explanation: The problem statement establishes the need for the grant—it must clearly identify and justify the problem's significance before proposing any solution.

quizQuestions.question: A project proposal's expected outcomes section should describe:
options: How long the project will take
Specific, measurable results the project will achieve
The names of all team members
The proposal writer's qualifications
quizQuestions.answer: Specific, measurable results the project will achieve
quizQuestions.explanation: Expected outcomes must be specific and measurable—they tell the funder what tangible results the project will produce, making success evaluable.

quizQuestions.question: Budget justification in a proposal means:
options: Listing the total cost without explanation
Explaining why each budget item is necessary and how much it will cost
Comparing your budget to other similar projects
Including only the largest expenses
quizQuestions.answer: Explaining why each budget item is necessary and how much it will cost
quizQuestions.explanation: Budget justification explains the rationale for each expense, showing funders that resources will be used efficiently and appropriately.

quizQuestions.question: A project timeline in a proposal serves to:
options: Show that the project will take a very long time
Demonstrate that the project is feasible within a defined period with specific milestones
List the qualifications of all team members
Explain the budget in visual form
quizQuestions.answer: Demonstrate that the project is feasible within a defined period with specific milestones
quizQuestions.explanation: A timeline shows funders that the project is realistically planned and executable, with clear milestones and a defined endpoint.

quizQuestions.question: A professional business email should always:
options: Begin with 'Hey' to sound approachable
Include a clear subject line, professional greeting, specific purpose, and appropriate closing
Be as brief as possible—a single sentence is always best
Avoid using bullet points or lists
quizQuestions.answer: Include a clear subject line, professional greeting, specific purpose, and appropriate closing
quizQuestions.explanation: Professional emails require a clear subject line, appropriate greeting (Dear + name), a specific and organized message, and a professional closing (e.g., 'Regards').

quizQuestions.question: In Professional Writing, A resume's purpose is to:
options: Tell your complete life story in chronological order
Present your skills, education, and experience concisely in a format that matches employer needs
Include every job or activity you have ever done
Be at least three pages long
quizQuestions.answer: Present your skills, education, and experience concisely in a format that matches employer needs
quizQuestions.explanation: A resume is a strategic marketing document—it selects and presents the most relevant qualifications for a specific opportunity, concisely and clearly.

quizQuestions.question: Which subject line is most useful for a professional information-request email?
options: Hello
Question
Request for Fall Internship Application Details
Important!!!
quizQuestions.answer: Request for Fall Internship Application Details
quizQuestions.explanation: A specific subject helps the recipient understand and route the request. The other choices do not satisfy the module definition or the evidence in the prompt.

quizQuestions.question: Which resume bullet uses the strongest evidence?
options: Helped with events
Coordinated three workshops for 60 participants and tracked attendance
Did many important tasks
Responsible for things
quizQuestions.answer: Coordinated three workshops for 60 participants and tracked attendance
quizQuestions.explanation: The bullet uses an action verb, scope, and measurable result. The other choices do not satisfy the module definition or the evidence in the prompt.

quizQuestions.question: A professional writing portfolio is curated by:
options: Including everything you have ever written
Selecting pieces that best represent your range, expertise, and strongest skills for a specific purpose
Choosing only the longest pieces you have written
Ordering pieces alphabetically by title
quizQuestions.answer: Selecting pieces that best represent your range, expertise, and strongest skills for a specific purpose
quizQuestions.explanation: Portfolio curation is strategic—selecting pieces that best demonstrate range, skill, and development for the specific audience reviewing the portfolio.

quizQuestions.question: Revising pieces to publication quality means:
options: Making pieces longer to show more effort
Ensuring every sentence, word choice, citation, and format is polished and error-free
Submitting the original first draft
Only fixing spelling and grammar
quizQuestions.answer: Ensuring every sentence, word choice, citation, and format is polished and error-free
quizQuestions.explanation: Publication-quality revision addresses all levels—content, argument, style, sentence-level clarity, and surface mechanics—until the piece represents your best work.

quizQuestions.question: A portfolio introduction should:
options: List every piece in the portfolio with word counts
Explain the writer's development, curation choices, and what the portfolio as a whole demonstrates
Be identical in style to all other portfolio pieces
Be written before the portfolio pieces are selected
quizQuestions.answer: Explain the writer's development, curation choices, and what the portfolio as a whole demonstrates
quizQuestions.explanation: A portfolio introduction provides a reflective overview—explaining the writer's growth, why specific pieces were chosen, and what the collection demonstrates about the writer's skills.

quizQuestions.question: Which curation choice best demonstrates growth in a writing portfolio?
options: Four unrelated first drafts
An early draft paired with a substantially revised version and reflection
Only the longest assignments
Every file created during the course
quizQuestions.answer: An early draft paired with a substantially revised version and reflection
quizQuestions.explanation: Draft-to-revision evidence makes development visible. The other choices do not satisfy the module definition or the evidence in the prompt.

quizQuestions.question: Which portfolio introduction sentence best explains a curation decision?
options: I paired my early feature draft with its revision to show how stronger attribution changed the article's credibility
This portfolio contains four files
I chose these pieces because they were already finished
The documents appear in alphabetical order
quizQuestions.answer: I paired my early feature draft with its revision to show how stronger attribution changed the article's credibility
quizQuestions.explanation: A useful portfolio introduction connects a selection to a specific learning outcome and evidence of growth. File counts, convenience, and alphabetical order describe the collection without interpreting development.

quizQuestions.question: A submission cover letter for a publication should:
options: Be identical regardless of which publication you are submitting to
Be specifically tailored to the publication's style, mission, and readership
Summarize the entire piece in detail
Focus on the writer's personal background rather than the work
quizQuestions.answer: Be specifically tailored to the publication's style, mission, and readership
quizQuestions.explanation: Each submission letter should be tailored to the specific publication—demonstrating familiarity with the outlet, its audience, and why this particular piece fits.

quizQuestions.question: Researching submission guidelines before submitting to a publication is important because:
options: All publications use identical formatting and length requirements
Each publication has specific requirements for format, length, and style that must be followed
Submission guidelines are optional suggestions only
Guidelines only matter for academic journals
quizQuestions.answer: Each publication has specific requirements for format, length, and style that must be followed
quizQuestions.explanation: Ignoring submission guidelines signals unprofessionalism and often results in automatic rejection; each outlet has specific requirements that must be followed exactly.

quizQuestions.question: What should a writer verify before tailoring a submission cover letter?
options: The outlet’s stated audience and submission requirements
The editor’s private contact details
Unverified rumors about acceptance rates
Whether the writer can ignore length limits
quizQuestions.answer: The outlet’s stated audience and submission requirements
quizQuestions.explanation: A responsible pitch aligns with published scope and guidelines. The other choices do not satisfy the module definition or the evidence in the prompt.

quizQuestions.question: A strong pitch letter should briefly explain:
options: The story angle, audience fit, and writer’s relevant preparation
The writer’s entire life history
Why guidelines should be ignored
Private details about the editor
quizQuestions.answer: The story angle, audience fit, and writer’s relevant preparation
quizQuestions.explanation: Editors need the proposed story, why it fits, and why the writer can deliver it.

questions.question: An editorial draft says only, “The library should improve because improvement is good.” Which revision task should come first?
options: Replace it with a specific, debatable claim that names the proposed change and stakes
Add a dramatic adjective to every noun
Insert an unattributed quotation before the sentence
Move the same sentence to the conclusion
questions.answer: Replace it with a specific, debatable claim that names the proposed change and stakes
questions.explanation: A specific thesis gives the editorial a position, scope, and reason that evidence can support. Adjectives, unattributed material, and relocation do not correct the underlying lack of a defensible claim.

questions.question: Adapting writing for different audiences requires changing:
options: Only the length of the piece
Vocabulary, tone, format, and examples to match the audience's background and needs
The factual information in the piece
Only the title and opening paragraph
questions.answer: Vocabulary, tone, format, and examples to match the audience's background and needs
questions.explanation: Effective audience adaptation adjusts vocabulary, tone, formality, format, and which examples or evidence will resonate—while keeping core facts consistent.

questions.question: A profile writer has three vivid anecdotes but no clear angle. What should the writer do first?
options: Choose the subject trait or insight the anecdotes collectively reveal
Place every anecdote in chronological order regardless of relevance
Add a dramatic quotation that was not in the packet
Remove attribution so the prose reads smoothly
questions.answer: Choose the subject trait or insight the anecdotes collectively reveal
questions.explanation: A profile's angle gives reporting a coherent purpose and determines which scenes, facts, and quotations belong. Chronology alone does not create focus, and invented or unattributed material violates reporting practice.

questions.question: Which evidence would best strengthen an editorial supporting a public-garden proposal?
options: Measured parking use, a documented budget, and an accessibility plan
The writer's belief that gardens are beautiful
An anonymous claim with no date or source
A description of unrelated parks in another country
questions.answer: Measured parking use, a documented budget, and an accessibility plan
questions.explanation: Relevant, verifiable evidence addresses feasibility and likely objections to the proposal. Personal taste, unattributed claims, and unrelated examples do not establish local need, cost, or equitable access.

questions.question: Narrative journalism requires that all scenes and details be:
options: Invented by the writer to improve the story
Based on observed or reported facts—never fabricated
Kept vague to protect sources
Written in the third person only
questions.answer: Based on observed or reported facts—never fabricated
questions.explanation: Narrative journalism's fundamental ethical requirement is that all reported scenes, details, and quotations are factually accurate—literary technique applied only to real facts.

questions.question: The nut graf in a feature article explains:
options: The nutritional content in a food feature
The broader significance and relevance of the story to the reader
All sources used in the piece
The journalist's personal opinion
questions.answer: The broader significance and relevance of the story to the reader
questions.explanation: The nut graf provides the 'so what'—the broader context and significance that explains why readers should care about the story.

questions.question: A narrative report has a vivid opening scene but delays the verified outage facts for five paragraphs. What revision best balances story and reporting?
questions.answer: Add an early nut graf that states what happened, when, where, and why the event matters, then return to the scene.
questions.explanation: A narrative lead may create interest, but readers still need timely factual orientation. An early nut graf supplies the verified event and significance without requiring the writer to abandon responsible scene-based storytelling.

questions.question: A professional LinkedIn post should be distinguished from an Instagram caption by its which of the following?
options: Professional audience, purpose, tone, and career-oriented context
Shorter character count
Requirement to avoid all personal reflection
Use of only images and no text
questions.answer: Professional audience, purpose, tone, and career-oriented context
questions.explanation: LinkedIn writing is shaped by professional audience expectations and career-related purpose.

questions.question: What is the key difference between a signed opinion column and a newspaper editorial?
options: A column presents the named writer’s view, while an editorial represents the publication’s institutional position
An editorial may use evidence, while a column may not
A column must be fictional, while an editorial must be factual
An editorial is always longer than a column
questions.answer: A column presents the named writer’s view, while an editorial represents the publication’s institutional position
questions.explanation: Authorship and represented voice distinguish the genres: a signed column belongs to its writer, while an editorial expresses the publication’s official or board position. Both still require responsible evidence and reasoning.

questions.question: The 'right of reply' principle in investigative journalism requires:
options: Allowing subjects to edit the article before publication
Giving subjects the opportunity to respond to findings before the story is published
Publishing only positive findings about investigation subjects
Keeping all sources confidential from the subject
questions.answer: Giving subjects the opportunity to respond to findings before the story is published
questions.explanation: Right of reply is the ethical obligation to give subjects of potentially damaging reporting a chance to respond, ensuring fairness in the reporting process.

questions.question: A social post includes an image of volunteers planting seedlings. Which alt text is most useful?
options: Three volunteers place tomato seedlings in a waist-high raised bed
Image of something nice
Photo—click here
Red and green colors
questions.answer: Three volunteers place tomato seedlings in a waist-high raised bed
questions.explanation: Useful alt text concisely communicates the image’s relevant content and action. Vague labels, calls to click, and color lists do not give a nonvisual reader the information needed to understand the post.

questions.question: A waste log and a staff interview point to different explanations for a decline in discarded food. What should the investigative writer do?
options: State the conflict, corroborate with additional records, and qualify the conclusion
Choose the more dramatic source and ignore the other
Combine both claims into one unattributed statement
Report causation because the waste total changed
questions.answer: State the conflict, corroborate with additional records, and qualify the conclusion
questions.explanation: Conflicting evidence should remain visible while the writer seeks corroboration and explains uncertainty. Selecting, blending, or overstating the sources would conceal the limits of the available record.

questions.question: Investigating a local issue as a journalist requires:
options: Only reading other newspaper articles about the topic
Gathering information from multiple sources including interviews, documents, and data
Writing only from personal experience
Publishing findings before any verification
questions.answer: Gathering information from multiple sources including interviews, documents, and data
questions.explanation: Investigative journalism requires multiple forms of evidence—interviews, documents, data—to build a complete, verifiable account of the issue being investigated.

questions.question: Which note most clearly separates verified fact from narrative description in a reported scene?
questions.answer: The timestamp and number of visitors come from the incident log; the description of phone lights comes from Ana Ruiz’s attributed quotation.
questions.explanation: A verification note names the source for each kind of detail so the reader can distinguish records and attributed observation from the writer’s own reconstruction. That boundary prevents invented scene detail.

questions.question: Consistency in social media writing for a cause or organization refers to:
options: Posting the exact same content every day
Maintaining a coherent brand voice, message, and visual identity across all posts and platforms
Using the same hashtags on every post
Posting only once per week
questions.answer: Maintaining a coherent brand voice, message, and visual identity across all posts and platforms
questions.explanation: Brand consistency in social media builds recognition and trust—a coherent voice, values, and messaging strategy across all content is essential.

questions.question: A pitch letter to a publication editor proposes which of the following?
options: A story idea, angle, relevance, and writer qualifications for the publication
A completed polished final draft for immediate publication
A private diary entry
A generic request with no audience or angle
questions.answer: A story idea, angle, relevance, and writer qualifications for the publication
questions.explanation: A pitch sells the idea and fit before the editor commits to the piece. Students need to recognize why A story idea, angle, relevance, and writer qualifications for the publication matches the evidence in the question and why nearby options do not.

questions.question: What best distinguishes the Module 12 portfolio from a folder of unrevised assignments?
options: It deliberately curates four pieces, revises them, and explains audience, craft choices, and growth
It includes every course file in chronological order
It uses one genre only and omits revision notes
It is completed in one sitting without feedback
questions.answer: It deliberately curates four pieces, revises them, and explains audience, craft choices, and growth
questions.explanation: The portfolio demonstrates range and development through purposeful selection, revision, annotations, and an introduction; simple file collection does not show those decisions.

questions.question: Which opening best suits an evidence-based opinion blog post?
options: A concise claim that states the issue, position, and why it matters to the intended reader
A numbered instruction before the problem is identified
A full autobiography unrelated to the issue
A list of links with no interpretation
questions.answer: A concise claim that states the issue, position, and why it matters to the intended reader
questions.explanation: An opinion post should establish its position and stakes for the audience, then develop evidence and reasoning. Step instructions belong to a how-to structure, while unrelated biography and unexplained links do not create an argument.

questions.question: Why are documents especially useful as evidence in investigative writing?
options: It is easier to obtain than human sources
It provides verifiable, primary evidence that is harder to dispute than memory or verbal claims
Readers always prefer documents to quotations
Documents require no interpretation
questions.answer: It provides verifiable, primary evidence that is harder to dispute than memory or verbal claims
questions.explanation: Documents provide concrete, verifiable facts—budgets, emails, records—that ground investigative findings in demonstrable evidence.

questions.question: A 90-second news script contains a 42-word sentence with three subordinate clauses. What is the best revision for listeners?
options: Split it into short sentences and repeat the key noun where a pronoun could be unclear
Add more subordinate clauses to sound formal
Move every fact into a parenthetical aside
Replace concrete nouns with abbreviations
questions.answer: Split it into short sentences and repeat the key noun where a pronoun could be unclear
questions.explanation: Listeners cannot reread a broadcast sentence, so short syntax and clear references reduce processing load. Extra clauses, asides, and unexplained abbreviations make a one-pass audio message harder to understand.

questions.question: For one fictional venue in Module 13, name two details a tailored cover letter must address and explain why each matters.
questions.answer: A strong response identifies two of the following and connects each to venue fit: the venue’s intended audience, accepted format or length, evidence requirements, or a revision the piece still needs. For example, City Voices requires a reported community feature and two attributed interviews, so the letter must state that interviews are not yet complete rather than inventing them.
questions.explanation: The task checks whether the writer can translate a venue profile into honest, specific submission choices without contacting a real outlet or claiming unfinished reporting is complete.

questions.question: When selecting four pieces for the Module 12 portfolio, which choice best demonstrates range and growth?
options: Choose pieces from different genres and explain how revisions improved audience and craft decisions
Choose four nearly identical first drafts because they require no explanation
Select only the shortest pieces and omit revision evidence
Include unrelated work without identifying its audience
questions.answer: Choose pieces from different genres and explain how revisions improved audience and craft decisions
questions.explanation: Range comes from purposeful genre variety, while growth must be shown through concrete revision choices and explanation rather than asserted.

questions.question: Proofreading professional documents before submission is critical because:
options: Spellcheck tools catch all possible errors
Errors in professional writing undermine credibility and can have real professional consequences
Professional readers never notice minor errors
Proofreading is only necessary for academic papers
questions.answer: Errors in professional writing undermine credibility and can have real professional consequences
questions.explanation: In professional contexts, errors signal lack of care and undermine credibility—they can affect career opportunities and professional relationships.

questions.question: What should an effective call to action do at the end of an opinion column?
options: Gives readers a clear, purposeful next step connected to the argument
Repeats the introductory hook word for word
Introduces an unrelated topic
Avoids asking the reader to think or act
questions.answer: Gives readers a clear, purposeful next step connected to the argument
questions.explanation: A call to action turns the column's argument into a clear next step for the audience.

questions.question: Portfolio range is best demonstrated by:
options: Writing the longest possible pieces
Including work across different genres, audiences, and purposes that shows versatility
Selecting only one genre and writing many examples of it
Including all work completed during the course
questions.answer: Including work across different genres, audiences, and purposes that shows versatility
questions.explanation: Range demonstrates versatility—the ability to write effectively across different genres (feature, opinion, script, professional) for different audiences and purposes.

questions.question: Receiving a rejection from a publication is most professionally handled by:
options: Abandoning the piece entirely
Reviewing any feedback, revising if needed, and submitting to another appropriate venue
Resubmitting the identical piece to the same outlet immediately
Complaining publicly about the editorial decision
questions.answer: Reviewing any feedback, revising if needed, and submitting to another appropriate venue
questions.explanation: Professional writers treat rejection as information—reviewing feedback, revising strategically, and resubmitting to other suitable venues.

questions.question: A proposal budgets $900 for six acoustic panels. Which sentence provides the strongest budget justification?
options: Six panels at $150 each reduce sound spill around the 40-seat quiet zone during the six-week pilot
Acoustic panels cost $900
The panels seem useful
Other libraries may own panels
questions.answer: Six panels at $150 each reduce sound spill around the 40-seat quiet zone during the six-week pilot
questions.explanation: A budget justification links quantity, unit cost, total cost, and project purpose. Repeating the total, offering an unsupported opinion, or discussing other libraries does not show why the expense is necessary and reasonable.

questions.question: Sound cues in a podcast script direct the audio producer to:
questions.answer: Add, fade, pause, layer, or adjust audio elements such as music, ambience, effects, and transitions.
questions.explanation: Sound cues are instructions for the production layer of the podcast, not decorative notes.

questions.question: What should the brief revision note required in the Module 12 portfolio show?
options: A specific change, the reason for it, and how it better serves audience or purpose
Only the final word count
A list of files with no discussion of changes
Praise for the draft without identifying a revision
questions.answer: A specific change, the reason for it, and how it better serves audience or purpose
questions.explanation: A useful revision note makes the writing process visible by linking an actual change to audience, genre, clarity, evidence, or craft.

questions.question: Submission guidelines for a publication must be followed because:
options: They are optional suggestions for experienced writers
Each outlet has specific requirements, and ignoring them signals unprofessionalism and leads to rejection
Guidelines only apply to academic journal submissions
All publications use the same universal format
questions.answer: Each outlet has specific requirements, and ignoring them signals unprofessionalism and leads to rejection
questions.explanation: Submission guidelines are requirements—not suggestions. Failing to follow them immediately signals unprofessionalism and typically results in rejection without reading.

questions.question: Which claim belongs in the Module 12 portfolio introduction?
options: Across these four pieces, my revisions show stronger audience control because I changed the science feature’s definitions and the podcast script’s sound cues.
Every piece is perfect, so no revision was needed.
The portfolio contains four files, and that fact alone proves growth.
My teacher’s opinion is the only evidence of my development.
questions.answer: Across these four pieces, my revisions show stronger audience control because I changed the science feature’s definitions and the podcast script’s sound cues.
questions.explanation: The portfolio introduction should make a growth claim and support it with concrete evidence from selected and revised work.

questions.question: Professional social media content planning requires which of the following?
options: A strategic content calendar aligned with audience, goals, platform, and voice
Posting spontaneously whenever inspiration strikes
Using the same message on every platform without revision
Avoiding analytics or audience feedback
questions.answer: A strategic content calendar aligned with audience, goals, platform, and voice
questions.explanation: Professional social media writing is planned around audience, purpose, timing, platform norms, and brand voice.

questions.question: A profile feature article uses which combination of techniques?
options: Only statistics and official reports about the subject
In-depth research, direct observation, quotations, anecdotes, and scene-setting to create a textured portrait
A simple interview transcript without narrative framing
Third-person voice with no direct quotations
questions.answer: In-depth research, direct observation, quotations, anecdotes, and scene-setting to create a textured portrait
questions.explanation: A strong profile uses multiple reporting and narrative techniques—observation, interviews, documents, anecdotes—to build a complex, human portrait of the subject.

questions.question: Tension in narrative journalism is created by:
options: Using angry or sensational language
Structuring the narrative around an unresolved conflict that compels readers forward
Including as many facts as possible
Avoiding any emotional content in the reporting
questions.answer: Structuring the narrative around an unresolved conflict that compels readers forward
questions.explanation: Narrative tension comes from structural choices—placing an unresolved question or conflict at the center of the story that readers are compelled to follow to resolution.

questions.question: A portfolio introduction provides value because it:
questions.answer: It frames the writer's goals, growth, selected pieces, and intended audience before readers evaluate the work.
questions.explanation: The introduction helps readers understand why the pieces were chosen and how to read the portfolio as evidence of growth.
